description: Learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

book.title: So Good They Can't Ignore You
book.author: Cal Newport

cards.title: Follow Your Passion Is a Trap
cards.subtitle: You quit your job to follow your passion. Six months in, you're broke and the passion feels like work.
body: Everyone said find what you love. So you did. Now you're doing it full-time and it turns out you hate the business side.
The people who love their work got good first. The love came after. Passion grows from competence, not soul-searching.
cards.takeaway: The treasure you're looking for doesn't exist yet—you have to build it.

cards.title: Craftsman Mindset Beats Passion Mindset
cards.subtitle: You spend Monday morning asking if your job fulfills you. Your coworker spends it getting better at the job.
body: The passion mindset is about what you get. The craftsman mindset is about what you give.

• One produces anxiety, the other produces skills
• Improvement is measurable, passion is not
• The clarity is the advantage
cards.takeaway: Only one of these people will still be here in five years enjoying the work.

cards.title: Career Capital Comes Before Control
cards.subtitle: You ask for remote work and flexible hours in the interview. They hire someone else who didn't ask for anything.
body: You want autonomy, interesting projects, the freedom to work from anywhere. Everyone does. The problem is you're asking before you have leverage.
The person who got the job will work on-site for two years, get good, then negotiate everything you wanted upfront.
cards.takeaway: Control without competence is called unemployment.

cards.title: Deliberate Practice Is Uncomfortable
cards.subtitle: You've been doing the same job for five years and you're not any better than you were at year two.
body: You hit a plateau and stayed there. Every day you do what you already know how to do. It feels fine. Comfortable.
The person who started after you is already better because they're still working at the edge of what they can't do yet.
cards.takeaway: Comfort means you stopped improving.

cards.title: Patience Beats Shortcuts
cards.subtitle: You've been looking for the fast path for three years. Your colleague who started when you did just got promoted.
body: You want the interesting work now. The recognition now. So you keep looking for the angle, the hack, the shortcut.
Meanwhile someone else just put their head down and got good. The shortcut fantasy keeps you switching paths.
cards.takeaway: Time in the game, done right, is the only advantage that compounds.

cards.title: Mission Requires a Foundation
cards.subtitle: You launch your mission-driven startup. No one cares because you don't have the skills to make it matter.
body: The mission felt purposeful. More meaningful than just getting good at something. So you skipped the boring part.

• No one pays attention to ambitious ideas from people who can't execute
• Without the foundation it's just a daydream with a blog
cards.takeaway: Missions don't make you valuable—they require that you already are.

cards.title: Adjacent Possible Is Where Missions Hide
cards.subtitle: You spend six months brainstorming your big career move. Someone at the frontier sees the opportunity in a week.
body: The mission won't reveal itself from your couch. You're trying to see what's possible from the outside looking in.
The person who's been building skills for years is standing at the cutting edge. They can see what's newly possible.
cards.takeaway: The adjacent possible is invisible until you're standing next to it.

cards.title: Little Bets Beat Grand Plans
cards.subtitle: You quit your job for the grand plan. Six months in, you realize it was the wrong plan and now you're broke.
body: The plan felt right. You thought about it for months. So you made the big move. Now you're committed to something that doesn't work.
The person who kept their job and ran small experiments already figured out what you're learning the expensive way.
cards.takeaway: Grand plans fail because they're too expensive to abandon.

cards.title: Remarkable Work Needs a Venue
cards.subtitle: You built something great. It's sitting on your hard drive. No one knows it exists.
body: The work is good. You know it's good. But it doesn't matter because it's not going anywhere.
Remarkable work needs a market that can notice and share it. The purple cow stands out in the field, not in your garage.
cards.takeaway: Quality without distribution is a hobby.

cards.title: Autonomy Without Capital Fails
cards.subtitle: You quit to freelance and gain freedom. Three months later you're taking any client who'll pay you.
body: Freedom sounded better than the job. So you left. Now you're scrambling for work, saying yes to projects you hate.

• Without rare skills, autonomy just means unemployed with extra steps
• Early autonomy feels like freedom, looks like struggle
cards.takeaway: Control is a perk you earn, not a starting condition.

cards.title: Passion Follows Mastery, Not the Other Way
cards.subtitle: You loved photography until you got good at spreadsheets. Now you think about spreadsheets on weekends.
body: The logic runs backward. You didn't start out loving this. You got good at it. Competence created confidence.
Being bad at something makes it hard to love. Being good at something makes it easier to care.
cards.takeaway: You love what you're good at, not the other way around.

cards.title: Most Jobs Don't Match Pre-Existing Passions
cards.subtitle: You like hiking, podcasts, and philosophy. The economy doesn't have a vague intellectual interests sector.
body: Your hobbies are great. They're also not jobs. Most fulfilling careers don't map to things you loved at 22.
The overlap between your passions and what the market values is mostly luck.
cards.takeaway: The career that fits comes after the skill, not before.

cards.title: Building Skills Unlocks Better Opportunities
cards.subtitle: You wanted remote work on day one. Three years later, you're good enough that companies compete to give it to you.
body: Career capital opens doors that credentials can't. The first year you asked for flexibility and got rejected.

• You built rare skills instead
• Now recruiters offer exactly what you wanted
• Companies compete to give control to experts
cards.takeaway: Build the skills first, shape the job second.

cards.title: Feedback Loops Accelerate Skill
cards.subtitle: You get feedback once a year at your review. You've been making the same mistake for eleven months.
body: If you only get feedback once a year, you improve once a year. The person in the other department gets it every week.
The speed of the loop determines the speed of growth. Tight loops mean you fail small and learn fast.
cards.takeaway: Seek environments where the loop is faster than annual.

cards.title: Most Courage Advice Skips the Capital
cards.subtitle: The entrepreneur on stage says be brave and quit your job. He spent eight years at Google first.
body: The advice sounds inspiring. Take the leap. Follow your dreams. Be courageous. What they skip is the boring part where they built leverage.
The people who make bold moves successfully usually spent years quietly building skills before anyone noticed.
cards.takeaway: Courage without competence is called recklessness.

cards.title: Skills Compound, Passion Doesn't
cards.subtitle: You've changed careers three times in five years chasing passion. Your college roommate is a VP now.
body: Passion is a feeling. Feelings fluctuate. Skills compound. What you master in year three builds on year two.
A decade in, you're not ten times better—you're exponentially better. But only if you stayed in the game.
cards.takeaway: Compounding requires staying long enough to see the curve.

cards.title: Lifestyle Design Requires Capital First
cards.subtitle: You want the four-hour workweek. You're working sixty hours because no one will pay you for four.
body: The laptop-on-the-beach life sounds perfect. You want it now. Problem is that life costs capital.

• Either money or reputation or skills rare enough that people pay you on your terms
• The lifestyle gurus already had the capital
cards.takeaway: The four-hour workweek is a finish line, not a starting point.

cards.title: The Market Doesn't Owe You Meaning
cards.subtitle: You want meaningful work. The market wants you to solve a problem it cares about. These aren't the same thing.
body: Meaningful work is rare and valuable. Which means you need to offer something rare and valuable in return.
The market isn't structured to hand you purpose. It's structured to reward people who solve expensive problems.
cards.takeaway: Create value first, negotiate meaning second.

cards.title: Quitting Restarts the Clock
cards.subtitle: You're three years in and it doesn't feel right, so you switch. Now you're back at zero.
body: It still didn't feel like your passion, so you left. Now you're starting over. The passion mindset creates serial restarts.
Compounding requires time in the same game. Switching feels like progress but resets your advantage.
cards.takeaway: They didn't find the perfect path. They just stayed on one.

cards.title: Good Careers Are Built, Not Found
cards.subtitle: You've been searching for your dream job for two years. It doesn't exist yet because you haven't built it.
body: The myth is that your perfect job is out there waiting to be discovered. The reality is you build it incrementally.
Stop searching. Start building. You create it by accumulating capital and trading it for control.
cards.takeaway: Construction beats discovery.
